artists.story: Practicing the sacred Kohbar and Mithila traditions since age 12, Meera Devi uses natural mineral and plant-based dyes extracted from crushed leaves, lampblack, and turmeric. Her works carry motifs of sacred flora, fertility, and cosmic balance passed down through five generations of women in her family.
artists.tradition: Centuries-old folk art from the Mithila region of Bihar, traditionally painted on freshly plastered mud walls during ceremonies, characterized by eye-catching geometrical patterns and natural pigment extraction.

artists.story: Ramesh learned the fragile art of Blue Pottery under his grandfather in Kot Jewar. Unlike conventional clay pottery, his works use Egyptian paste made of quartz powder, powdered glass, Fuller’s earth, and natural gum, fired only once at low temperatures to produce an inimitable glassy turquoise luster.
artists.tradition: A distinct craft of Jaipur of Turko-Persian origin, famous for using no clay whatsoever, creating translucent, cobalt and copper-tinted decorative vessels and tiles.

artists.story: A master embroiderer from the nomadic Rabari and Ahir communities of Kutch, Lalita Ben stitches intricate mirrors (abhala) into hand-dyed cotton fabrics, creating wearable heirlooms that tell the migration and kinship stories of her community.
artists.tradition: An embroidery signature of the arid Kutch desert in Gujarat, known for vibrant silk threadwork, geometric herringbone stitches, and hand-cut mirrors that reflect moonlight.

artists.story: Using rice paste paste pigment on mud-coated walls and handmade canvas, Jivya depicts the rhythm of agricultural cycles, sacred Tarpa dances, and reverence for Mother Nature.
artists.tradition: Tribal art originating from Maharashtra, Warli paintings communicate through basic geometric forms: circles, triangles, and squares representing celestial bodies, mountains, and human community.

artists.story: Radha weaves gossamer-light sarees combining silk and cotton with real zari borders on traditional pit looms, sustaining a centuries-old royal weaving patronage.
artists.tradition: Chanderi weaves are celebrated for lightweight sheer texture and opulent floral motifs woven entirely on wooden handlooms.

creativeJourneys.title: The Living Genesis of Tree of Life: An Artisan's Odyssey
creativeJourneys.introduction: Every sacred piece of Madhubani Painting begins long before the first stroke touches the canvas. It begins with inherited memories, mindful preparation of organic elements, and quiet devotion to ancestral lineage. Follow the step-by-step unfolding of "Tree of Life" from inception to completion.
creativeJourneys.fullStory: The creation of "Tree of Life" exemplifies the unhurried patience of Madhubani Painting. Stage 1 (Inspiration): Spiritual reflection on nature Stage 2 (Natural Dyes): Grinding plant dyes and minerals Stage 3 (Final Linework): Traditional bamboo pen lineation Each layer preserves hours of dedicated craftsmanship, celebrating the profound synergy between human hand and natural world. The final piece stands not merely as an aesthetic achievement, but as a living bridge between generations of tradition.

exhibitions.title: Traditional Indian Art: Echoes of the Ancestral Hand
exhibitions.subtitle: A curated virtual retrospective exploring the timeless geometry, organic pigments, and folk spiritualism of Madhubani Painting.
exhibitions.description: This virtual exhibition brings together 1 signature creations by Meera Devi, including "Tree of Life". Rooted in the rich cultural tapestry of Traditional Indian Art, each piece invites patrons into an unhurried sanctuary where ancient technique converges with quiet contemplation. Through natural minerals, sacred geometry, and inherited memory, the collection celebrates India's enduring artisan lineage.
